## Simple Dataset

\begin{columns}[T]

\begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}

We have a simple "volcano" dataset that has 20 elevation measurements that we got from R. 

**Variables:**

- **X (Predictor):** Grid position along mountain
- **Y (Response):** Elevation in meters

We are trying to predict elevation using the position

\end{column}




\begin{column}{0.50\textwidth}
```{r plots, echo = FALSE, results='asis'}
data(volcano)

peak_row <- which(volcano == max(volcano), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, "row"]
#Select the x's and y's
volc <- data.frame(x = 1:ncol(volcano),
                   y = volcano[peak_row, ])

x <- seq(1, 58, by = 3)
y <- volcano[20, x]



df <- data.frame(x, y)

#Split in half to fit on slide
df <- data.frame(x1 = x[1:10], y1 = y[1:10], x2 = x[11:20], y2 = y[11:20])

knitr::kable(df, col.names = c("X", "Y", "X", "Y"), format = "latex")
```

\end{column}

\end{columns}

## The Problem with Linear Regression

Linear regression models the relationship between a predictor and a response using a straight line.

$$
\hat{Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

Where:

- $\hat{y}$ = Predicted response (elevation)
- $\beta_0$ = Intercept
- $\beta_1$ = Slope
- $x$ = Predictor (grid position)

**Limitation** Linear regression assumes a constant slope across all the data



## When Data Isn't Linear

Let's visualize our volcano elevation data.

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width = "50%", fig.align="center"}
plot(x, y, pch = 19, type = "b", xlab = "Grid Position", ylab = "Elevation (meters)", main = "Volcano Elevation")
```

**Observation:** Elevation first increases, peaks, and then decreases

A straight line does not accurately capture this

## Fitting a Linear Regression

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width = "50%", fig.align="center"}
model <- lm(y ~ x)

plot(x, y, pch = 19, type = "b", xlab = "Grid Position", ylab = "Elevation (meters)", main = "Volcano Elevation")

abline(model, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

**Observe:** The fitted regression line is nearly horizontal even though our data clearly increases and then decreases.

## Why Does Linear Regression Fail?

Linear Regression assumes a constant slope across all values of X.

$$
\hat{Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

**In our volcano dataset:**

- Elevation initially increases
- It reaches a peak
- It decreases
- Linear regression only estimates one slope for the whole dataset
- Both trends just get cancelled out, and leave us with a single horizontal line

**Conclusion** A single line cannot capture a relationship that changes direction.



## Introducing MARS 

**Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) ** is a regression model that can account for nonlinear relationships.

Unlike ordinary linear regression, MARS:

- Sections off regions using **knots**
- Fits separate slopes into every region
- Can automatically determine the points that divide each region
- Combines each region into a single function

**Key idea:** MARS allows us to fit multiple slopes into one, and allows it to change where needed.


## What is a Knot?

A **knot** is a point where the relationship between X and Y changes the slope.

- Knots are the point that divide our regions
- Each region has a unique slope
- MARS automatically determines where these knots are placed

In our dataset:

Elevation initially increased until it peaked, and then decreased.

So a knot at the peak would allow us to have 2 separate regions with 2 different slopes.

## Visualizing the Knot
```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width = "75%", fig.align="center"}

plot(x, y, pch = 19, type = "b", xlab = "Grid Position", ylab = "Elevation (meters)", main = "Visual of the Knot")

abline(v = 31, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
```

## Hinge Functions

MARS uses **hinge functions** to model the slopes within each section divided by a knot.

Two hinge functions are created around a knot $t$:

$$
h_1(x) = \max(0, t-x)
$$

$$
h_2(x) = \max(0, x-t)
$$
Where:

- $x$ = Predictor Value
- $t$ = Knot location
- $\max()$ = Returns the larger of the two values

**Key Idea:** Each hinge function is 0 on one side of the knot and increases/decreases on the other


## Visualizing Hinge Functions

```{r, hinge, echo=FALSE, fig.width = 9, fig.height=4, fig.show='hold', out.width = "90%", fig.align="center"}

knot <- 31
h1 <- pmax(0, knot - x)
h2 <- pmax(0, x - knot)


#Helps place side by side
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))


#Left hinge
plot(x, h1, type = "b", col = "blue", xlab = "X", ylab = "Hinge Value", main = "Left Hinge")
abline(v = knot, col = "red")

#Right hinge
plot(x, h2, type = "b", col = "blue", xlab = "X", ylab = "Hinge Value", main = "Right Hinge")

abline(v = knot, col = "red")
```


## Combining Hinge Functions

MARS combines multiple hinge functions into one to model the relationship between X and Y


$$
\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\max(0,t-x) + \beta_2\max(0,x-t)
$$


By combining these functions, we can model the separate slopes on each side of every knot while keeping the prediction line continuous


## Piecewise Regression

We can break up the MARS function into 2 separate piecewise linear models too.

$$ 
   \hat{y} =
   \begin{cases}
   \beta_0 + \beta_1(t-x), & x < t \\[5pt]
   \beta_0 + \beta_2(x-t), & x \ge t
   \end{cases}
$$

- **Left of the knot:** The model has a single linear relationship

- **Right of the knot:** The model has another single linear relationship

- **At the knot:** We can see where the 2 pieces combine to maintain continuity


## Polynomial Regression

Polynomial regression allows to model more complex models past simple linearity.

Quadratic Model Formula:

$$
\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2x^2
$$
- **Linear Regression:** Fits a single line through the data

- **Polynomial Regression:** Fits a curve using higher degree terms

- **Comparison:** We will be comparing to see how polynomial regression, which uses a single curve, compares to MARS, which uses hinge functions to model different regions of the data. 



## Introducing the Dataset

We will use the airquality dataset which has daily weather observations from New York City between May and September 1973.

**Variables:**

- **X (Predictor):** Day of observation (1 - 153)
- **Y (Response):** Daily maximum temperature (°F)

**Goal:** Model how temperature changes over time and compare polynomial regression vs MARS.

```{r weather, echo=FALSE}
data(airquality)

weather <- airquality
weather$DayIndex <- 1:nrow(weather)
```

## Polynomial Regression vs MARS

```{r, polynomial_mars, echo=FALSE, out.width = "60%", fig.align="center", warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, error=FALSE}
library(earth)
#Split data
set.seed(1)
training_idx <- sort(sample(1:nrow(weather), 0.7 * nrow(weather)))

train <- weather[training_idx, ]
test <- weather[-training_idx, ]

#Fit both models
poly_model <- lm(Temp ~ DayIndex + I(DayIndex^2), data = train)
mars_model <- earth(Temp ~ DayIndex, data = train)

plot(weather$DayIndex, weather$Temp, pch = 19, xlab = "Day", ylab = "Temperature (°F)", main = "Polynomial Regression vs MARS")

lines(train$DayIndex, fitted(poly_model), col = "blue", lwd = 3)
lines(train$DayIndex, fitted(mars_model), col = "red", lwd = 3)

legend("topright", legend = c("Polynomial Model", "MARS Model"), col = c("blue", "red"))
```

## Polynomial Regression vs MARS Results

We now evaluate the models using our test data

- **RMSE:** Lower is better.
- **R-squared** Higher is better.

```{r, model_results, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, error=FALSE}
poly_predict <- predict(poly_model, test)
mars_predict <- predict(mars_model, test)

#Evaluate metrics
poly_rmse <- sqrt(mean((test$Temp - poly_predict)^2))
mars_rmse <- sqrt(mean((test$Temp - mars_predict)^2))

poly_r2 <- 1 - sum((test$Temp - poly_predict)^2) / sum((test$Temp - mean(test$Temp))^2)
mars_r2 <- 1 - sum((test$Temp - mars_predict)^2) / sum((test$Temp - mean(test$Temp))^2)

results <- data.frame(Model = c("Polynomial", "MARS"), RMSE = c(poly_rmse, mars_rmse), R_Squared = c(poly_r2, mars_r2))

knitr::kable(results, format = "latex")

```


## Why Use MARS?

- **Capture Nonlinear relationships:** We are able to model patterns that simple linear regression can miss

- **Automatic Knot Selection:** MARS automatically identifies the point where relationships change 

- **Flexible Modeling:** MARS can capture different slopes and incorporate interactions between predictors

- **Controls overfitting:** Because we use backwards pruning and Generalized Cross Validation (GCV), we can cut back on overly complex models


## Forward Selection

- **RSS for hinge pairs:** Starting from an intercept-only model, MARS fits a model with each candidate hinge pair (every predictor × every candidate knot) and stores its RSS

- **Minimize RSS:** MARS compares these models and keeps the hinge pair with the lowest RSS

- **Repeat:** Using the new model as the base, MARS searches all candidates again and adds the hinge pair that lowers RSS the most

- **Build overfitted model:** This continues until a maximum number of terms is reached or RSS stops improving, deliberately overfitting so the backward pass can prune


## Finding the Best Knot 
x and t are the observed values of the data

$$
x = \{x_1, x_2, x_3\}, \qquad t \in \{x_1, x_2, x_3\}
$$

Build the pairs:

$$
h_1(x) = \max(0,\, t - x), \qquad h_2(x) = \max(0,\, x - t)
$$

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
t & \hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 h_1(x) + \beta_2 h_2(x) & \text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \\
\hline
x_1 & \beta_0 + \beta_1(x_1 - x)_+ + \beta_2(x - x_1)_+ & \text{RSS}_1 \\
x_2 & \beta_0 + \beta_1(x_2 - x)_+ + \beta_2(x - x_2)_+ & \text{RSS}_2 \\
x_3 & \beta_0 + \beta_1(x_3 - x)_+ + \beta_2(x - x_3)_+ & \text{RSS}_3 \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$


MARS selects the knot with the smallest RSS, $t^* = \arg\min_k \text{RSS}_k$, and adds that hinge pair to the model.


## Building a Complex Model
```{r more-hinges, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
sizes  <- c(3, 5, 7, 21)   # max terms = intercept + 1, 2, 3, 10 pairs
labels <- c("1 pair max", "2 pairs max", "3 pairs max", "10 pairs max")
yl     <- range(volc$y) + c(-10, 10)

par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (k in seq_along(sizes)) {
  # forward pass only: no pruning, keep adding until nk terms
  fit   <- earth(y ~ x, data = volc, nk = sizes[k], thresh = 0, pmethod = "none")
  knots <- fit$cuts[fit$selected.terms[-1], "x"]
  
  plot(volc$x, volc$y, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "gray60",
       xlab = "Column", ylab = "Height", ylim = yl,
       main = paste0(labels[k], "\nRSS = ", round(fit$rss, 1)))
  abline(v = unique(knots), col = "red", lty = 2)
  lines(volc$x, predict(fit), col = "blue", lwd = 3)
}
```

\normalsize

## Building a Complex Model: Output

```{r more-hinges-plot, ref.label="more-hinges", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.2, out.width="100%"}
```

- Each new hinge pair adds a knot (red) where the slope can change
- RSS decreases with every pair added

## The Problem of Overfitting

\scriptsize
```{r overfit, echo =TRUE, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(4654)
noisy   <- volc
noisy$y <- volc$y + rnorm(nrow(volc), 0, 5)   # add noise

good <- earth(y ~ x, data = noisy, nk = 41, thresh = 0,
              minspan = 1, endspan = 1)                     # pruned
over <- earth(y ~ x, data = noisy, nk = 41, thresh = 0,
              minspan = 1, endspan = 1, pmethod = "none")   # no pruning

show_fit <- function(f, name, col) {
  mse <- mean((predict(f, volc) - volc$y)^2)              # vs. true heights
  plot(noisy$x, noisy$y, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "gray60",
       xlab = "Column", ylab = "Height",
       main = sprintf("%s: %d hinges\nRSS = %.0f, True MSE = %.1f",
                      name, length(f$selected.terms) - 1, f$rss, mse))
  lines(volc$x, predict(f), col = col, lwd = 3)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
show_fit(good, "Pruned",  "blue")
show_fit(over, "Overfit", "red")
```
\normalsize

## The Problem of Overfitting: Output

```{r overfit-plot, ref.label="overfit", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.6, out.width="100%"}
```

- **Overfit model:** many extra hinges bend to follow random noise, not the volcano's shape
- **Lower training RSS, but higher error against the true heights** 
- **Pruned model:** fewer hinges capture the real shape and ignore the noise

## Backwards Pruning

- **Remove each term:** Starting from the overfit forward model, MARS builds a set of new models, each with one term removed (the intercept is never removed)

- **Compare RSS:** It keeps the model whose removed term causes the smallest increase in RSS

- **Save and repeat:** The chosen model is saved, and the process repeats from it, removing one term at a time until only the intercept remains

- **Pruned model:** MARS computes the GCV of the saved model at each size and selects the one with the lowest GCV


## Backwards Pruning Cont.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Size} & \text{Candidate model} & \Delta\text{RSS} & \text{GCV (winner)} \\
\hline
M & \beta_0 + \beta_1(t_1-x)_+ + \beta_2(x-t_1)_+ + \beta_3(t_2-x)_+ & 0 & \text{GCV}_M \\
\hline
    & \mathbf{\beta_0 + \beta_1(t_1-x)_+ + \beta_2(x-t_1)_+} & \mathbf{\Delta_1} & \\
M-1 & \beta_0 + \beta_1(t_1-x)_+ + \beta_3(t_2-x)_+ & \Delta_2 & \text{GCV}_{M-1} \\
    & \beta_0 + \beta_2(x-t_1)_+ + \beta_3(t_2-x)_+ & \Delta_3 & \\
\hline
M-2 & \mathbf{\beta_0 + \beta_1(t_1-x)_+} & \mathbf{\Delta_4} & \text{GCV}_{M-2} \\
    & \beta_0 + \beta_2(x-t_1)_+ & \Delta_5 & \\
\hline
M-3 & \beta_0 \ \text{(intercept only)} & \Delta_6 & \text{GCV}_{M-3} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$


## Generalized Cross-Validation (GCV)

$$
\mathrm{GCV}(M) = \frac{\mathrm{RSS}(M)}{n\left(1 - \frac{C(M)}{n}\right)^2},
\qquad
C(M) = M + d\,K
$$
\noindent where
\begin{itemize}
  \item $n$ is the number of observations,
  \item $M$ is the number of terms (coefficients) in the model, including the intercept,
  \item $K$ is the number of distinct knots in the model,
  \item $d$ is the penalty per knot, typically $d = 2$ for additive models and $d = 3$ when interactions are allowed,
  \item $\mathrm{RSS}(M) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \hat{f}_M(x_i)\right)^2$ is the residual sum of squares,
  \item $\hat{f}_M(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} \beta_m B_m(x)$ is the fitted MARS model, where each basis function $B_m(x)$ is a hinge function or a product of hinge functions,
  \item $C(M) = M + dK$ is the effective number of parameters.
\end{itemize}
